Netherlands shipping guide

LoloBuy Shipping to the Netherlands: Costs, QC and Customs Checklist

Independent buyer guide

For a parcel going to the Netherlands, the item price is only one part of the budget. You may also need to account for delivery within China, payment charges, optional warehouse services, international transport, VAT, import duties and handling charges. The exact amount depends on your products, transaction, parcel and the information shown when you order.

This independent guide helps you keep those decisions separate. It describes a buyer’s checklist, not a guaranteed LoloBuy route, price or delivery date. The customs section reflects public Dutch Customs information checked on 5 November 2026; rules can change, so confirm the current position for your own shipment before you pay.

Start with the item and its source

A spreadsheet is useful for finding candidates, but an old row does not establish current stock or the contents of an order. Open the live product record and check the item, seller, variant, size and quantity. Save the source link and a note of the option you selected. For clothing, retain the seller’s size chart and any explanation of where the measurements begin and end.

Check whether the advertised price is for the item you selected rather than a smaller accessory or different version. Confirm the currency and any displayed domestic delivery cost. If the source page is unclear, record the uncertainty and seek clarification before payment; a warehouse photo later cannot repair an order that was placed for the wrong option.

Understand the two transport stages

LoloBuy’s public site describes a product-link workflow, warehouse inspection and international shipping. The seller-to-warehouse journey within China and the later journey to the Netherlands are separate stages. A seller’s domestic dispatch status is not the same thing as an international carrier’s acceptance scan.

Keep a record of the item order and, later, the parcel separately. A product may be awaiting seller dispatch while another has already arrived at the warehouse. Check the account’s live status and the exact service offered for each item. Do not interpret an old screenshot from another user as a current guarantee of timing or availability.

Review the available QC evidence

Before approving an item for a parcel, compare available inspection photographs with your order record. Check the visible colour, quantity, size label, model and any obvious marks. For shoes, compare both items and their visible labels. For a garment, check the relevant size label and, where a useful measurement image is available, whether its method matches the seller’s chart.

If a missing view would affect your decision, ask for a specific photograph only if the current service offers it. Name the feature or both measurement endpoints, and check any displayed fee first. Photos can document visible characteristics; they cannot by themselves prove authenticity, hidden construction, material composition, electronic function or personal fit.

If the product appears inconsistent, preserve the listing, selected option and relevant images. Describe the discrepancy factually and ask support what applies to that order before submitting the international parcel. Return and exchange eligibility can depend on the seller, the order stage and current terms; it should not be assumed from a photograph alone.

Build the cost estimate in layers

Start with the actual item amounts shown for your choices. Add any separately displayed domestic freight and payment or currency-conversion charges. Then list warehouse services you deliberately select, such as additional photographs, repacking or protection if offered. Mark unavailable prices as unknown rather than replacing them with another buyer’s figures.

International freight belongs in a separate line. The quoted amount may depend on the destination, route, contents, weight, dimensions and chosen options. A parcel’s final packed size can differ from the sum of the individual item measurements. Compare competing quotes for the same contents and destination, and note the date and the assumptions for each quote.

Finally add a destination-cost section for VAT, any applicable import duty, handling and carrier charges. Ask which costs are already included and which may be collected later. Do not add the same VAT or service twice, but do not assume a charge is prepaid unless the transaction record or provider confirms it. Keep the final estimate as a range when key amounts remain unknown.

Read actual and chargeable weight carefully

The physical weight of a packed parcel is only one input a carrier may use. A bulky, light parcel can be assessed differently if the selected line uses dimensional or volumetric weight. The applicable formula and divisor depend on the carrier or line; use the method shown for your actual route instead of importing a number from an unrelated example.

For a fair comparison, check the final length, width, height and scale weight using the same units. Compare an option with shoe boxes to an option without them only after considering protection, seller terms and any effect on returns. A cheaper preliminary quote is not a reliable total if the final dimensions, packaging or item restrictions are different.

Netherlands import costs: check the current rules

Dutch Customs says private buyers ordering from outside the EU may face VAT, import duties, excise where applicable and clearance-related charges. It distinguishes costs set by the sender from charges that may arise around import. Whether a seller or carrier collects an amount at checkout or later depends on the transaction; keep the order confirmation and invoice so you can check what was paid.

As of the Dutch Customs information updated 2 November 2026, declarants pay a €3 import duty per product category for qualifying e-commerce consignments with a value up to and including €150. From 1 November 2026, a €2 European handling fee per product category also applies to qualifying e-commerce consignments, including those over €150. Dutch Customs states that VAT is charged on these amounts and that the declaring company may pass costs to the buyer. These charges are not a universal fixed price per parcel or per individual product.

Those amounts should not be confused with the carrier’s own clearance or service charge. Classification, value, origin, exceptions and the precise transaction matter, and rules change. Check Dutch Customs and the actual seller or carrier’s current information for your case. This site does not determine your customs declaration or promise a particular result.

Compare lines using the same parcel

Before choosing a shipping line, list the destination, contents, packed dimensions, chargeable weight, quoted price and date. Then read the current restrictions: a route that accepts clothing may have different conditions for batteries, liquids or other goods. Check tracking coverage and any compensation or protection terms displayed for that line.

Do not choose solely by a historical transit claim. An estimate is not a delivery guarantee, and two parcels can experience different processing. Compare the complete cost and conditions that apply to your own parcel, not a quote for a different country or an old weight. If a requirement is unclear, ask the provider before paying.

Keep payment and tracking evidence

Save the order record, parcel contents, shipping selection and payment confirmation privately. After dispatch, keep the platform parcel reference and any carrier tracking number separate: they can describe different parts of the process. Read the latest status in the context of the carrier’s actual handoffs rather than assuming every parcel receives identical scans.

If a message asks you to pay a customs or redelivery charge, independently open the carrier’s official site or app and verify the tracking reference there. Avoid entering payment details through an unexpected message link. A legitimate request still needs to match your parcel, the party collecting the fee and the amount shown in a verified channel.

Before you submit the parcel

  1. Confirm each item’s selected option, quantity and available QC evidence.
  2. Resolve material mismatches while the item is still at the appropriate order stage.
  3. Record item, domestic, optional service and international costs separately.
  4. Check packed dimensions, route restrictions and the quote for your destination.
  5. Identify any VAT, duty, handling or carrier charge already paid or still unknown.
  6. Save receipts and tracking information privately, then verify later payment requests independently.

The most useful shipping estimate is not a single copied number. It is a dated record of the items, packaging, route and known charges, with unknown costs clearly marked. Update it when the parcel is packed and the current checkout information becomes available.
